1:
Ellicott pictures the moment of dictation. The parchment in the prison room at Rome, on which Luke was probably writing to the Apostle's dictation, was nearly filled up, so that what remained to be said must be brief; and Paul would have those last words introduced by a most impressive preface. The Greek is more accurately rendered, I solemnly charge thee, before those divine witnesses, the Eternal Father and the Blessed Son — present with the writer in his prison, and present equally with Timothy in his study-chamber or church in Asia. Henry finds the solemnity necessary rather than ornamental: the best of men have need to be awed into the discharge of their duty, for the work of a minister is not an indifferent thing but absolutely necessary, and woe be to him if he preach not the gospel. Calvin reads the charge as exhibiting God to Timothy as the avenger and Christ as the judge, if he should cease to discharge his office of teaching. As God showed by an inestimable pledge, when he spared not his only-begotten Son, how great is the care he has for the Church, so he will not suffer the negligence of pastors to remain unpunished, through whom souls that he redeemed at so costly a price perish or are exposed as a prey.

Gill names the first party from the side of Timothy's accountability: God, whose word the Scriptures are and by whom they are inspired, who had made Timothy an able minister of the New Testament. Clarke puts the same relation in two offices — before God, whose herald thou art, and before the Lord Jesus Christ, whose salvation thou art to proclaim, and who is coming to judge the world, all found then alive and all that have died from the foundation of the world. Barnes explains the old word: quick means living, and the idea is that Christ will be alike the Judge of all who are alive when he comes and of all who have died. He then draws the practical force out of it. In view of the fact that all, whether preachers or hearers, must give up their account to the final Judge, Paul charges Timothy to be faithful; and nothing conduces more to fidelity than the thought that we must soon account for the manner in which we have discharged it. Calvin says the same in a sentence: the living and the dead are those whom Christ shall find still alive at his coming and those who shall have died, so that none escape him.

The last clause turns on a reading. Robertson notes that the older text has "and" rather than "at", so that the nouns stand in the accusative of conjuration used after verbs of swearing — Timothy is adjured by the appearing and by the kingdom. Ellicott adopts the same restoration and holds that the passage gains immeasurably in strength by it: I charge thee in the sight of God and Jesus Christ, who will judge quick and dead, by his appearing and by his kingdom. The appearing is the coming a second time to judge the earth in the glory of the Father with his angels; the kingdom is that which, in the words of the creed, shall have no end, and which begins at that manifestation. Timothy is adjured by the one, before which he must stand, and by the other, in which he hoped to share. Ellicott hears in the ringing adjuration the germs of one of the ancient creeds. Barnes reads it more soberly: we need not suppose a visible realm set up on earth, but only an illustrious display of Christ as king, and of the extent and majesty of the empire over which he presides. Wesley keeps the received rendering, taking it of the appearing in the kingdom of glory.
2:
Gill takes the word to be preached as either Christ the essential Word, who is the sum and substance of the Gospel ministry, or the word of truth and faith; and it is to be published as heralds proclaim the will of their princes, openly, publicly and with a loud voice, without adding to it or taking from it, speaking out the whole and keeping back no part. Ellicott hears the same image in the verb and sets its opposite beside it: Timothy is to proclaim loudly and publicly, as a herald would announce the accession of his king, and the exact contrary is what Isaiah describes when he calls God's watchmen dumb dogs that cannot bark, sleeping, lying down, loving to slumber. He notes that the language of the original here is abrupt and emphatic, written evidently under strong emotion and with intense earnestness. Robertson identifies the form as an aorist imperative and observes that the word stands here absolutely, without qualification. Barnes makes the same charge the whole business of a life: this was to be the main work of Timothy's life, and Paul solemnly presses it upon him in view of the certain coming of the Redeemer to judgment.

The next command is a pun in Greek, and the commentators differ over how to take it. Robertson calls the two adverbs a play upon the word for season, since there are all sorts of seasons, some difficult and some easy, and reads the verb as take a stand, stand up to it, stick to it. Ellicott reports that some would give the word the sense of drawing nigh to, supplying the brethren or the Christian assemblies as its object, but thinks it better understood as an injunction to be earnest and urgent in the whole work of the ministry — press on, in season, out of season. What that means, he paraphrases: set apart no definite and fixed hours, no appointed times; the work must be done at all hours, not only in church, not merely in times of security and peace, but in the midst of dangers, even if thou art a prisoner and in chains, even if death threaten thee. He cites Chrysostom's encouragement to labour on in spite of apparent failure, since fountains flow on though none come to draw and rivers run though none drink at them, and Augustine's neater division, that in season refers to the willing and out of season to the unwilling — which Ellicott thinks touches only a part of Paul's thought.

Barnes separates the two words our version renders reprove and rebuke. The first implies only that a man may be in error and needs arguments presented to convince him of the truth, and carries no claim of authority in the one who does it; he presents reasons, and the force lies in them. The second implies authority, and means that we may say a thing is wrong and administer a rebuke for it as if there were no doubt that it was wrong, the propriety resting on our warrant to speak rather than on the arguments we produce, since men often know already that they are doing wrong and need no reasoning to convince them. So the minister is not merely to reason about sin, but may solemnly admonish men not to do it and warn them of the consequences. Clarke assigns each word a case: confute the false teacher, reprove cuttingly and severely those who will not abandon their sins, and comfort the feeble-minded, the diffident and the tempted. Ellicott adds that the reproof is not merely for those erring in doctrine but generally for the blameworthy, and that the last word is the sharper of the two. Wesley reads the whole as continual urging: not only when a fair occasion is given, but when there is none, one must be made.
3:
Gill dates the prophecy loosely: the time referred to was future when the Apostle wrote, but came on quickly, and the characters of it have appeared more or less in every age since. Ellicott explains why the warning was needed. Timothy must bear in mind that things in the Church on earth will not change for the better; the great drag-net, in its wide sweep, would keep drawing into its meshes something of every kind, and errors then just apparent would attain more formidable dimensions. The thirst for novelties in doctrine, and the desire for a teaching which, while offering peace to a troubled conscience, would yet allow the old self-indulgent life to go on as before, would increase; and in full view of that development, in sure expectation of a future full of anxious care, Timothy and his brother teachers must be wakeful, watchful and earnest. The very knowledge of the growing unpopularity of the sound doctrine must serve as an incentive to greater labour and more loving activity. Robertson makes the connection back to the previous verse: this coming time is one of the out-of-season times for which Timothy has just been told to be ready.

The two figures in the verse are given close attention. Barnes glosses the first as healthful doctrine, that which contributes to the health of the soul, and explains that at such a time men would seek instruction more conformable to their wishes, such as would palliate their evil propensities and deal gently with their vices — speak unto us smooth things, prophesy deceits. Of the second he notes that the verb rendered heap occurs nowhere else in the New Testament and means to accumulate, and that the word rendered itching, likewise unique, means to rub or scratch and then to tickle, the image being of the desire, when there is an itching sensation, to have it rubbed. Robertson adds that Clement of Alexandria tells of speakers tickling the ears of those who want to be tickled, and calls this the standing temptation of the merely popular preacher, to furnish the latest tickle. Clarke reads the same appetite as endless curiosity, an insatiable desire of variety, so that the hearers get their ears tickled with the language and accent of the speaker, abandoning the good and faithful preacher for the fine one; and he adds that interested men find their account in such a disposition, setting up for teachers and widening the way to ruin, taking care to soothe the passions and flatter the vices of a trifling people.

Barnes is careful about the agency in the turning away: it is the people themselves who turn from the truth, and the verse does not mean that the teachers turn them away by the influence of their instructions. Gill says only that they were not able to bear the hearing of the solid truths of the Gospel. Clarke explains why: the truth strips them of their vices, sacrifices their idols, darts its lightnings against their easily besetting sins, and absolutely requires a conformity to a crucified Christ, and therefore they turn their ears away from it; whereupon they will believe any kind of nonsense, since those who reject the truth are abandoned by the just judgment of God to credit the most degrading absurdities. Ellicott reads the same as a punishment rather than a mere consequence — this was the punishment of those who would listen only to what pleased them and flattered instead of reproving their way of life; they became involved in the various errors then taught in the schools of the heretics, and ended by turning away from every Christian truth. Wesley notes the same crowd of teachers appearing among them, and suspects that they send out one another, so that they are never at a loss for numbers.
5:
The first word is not quite what our version makes it. Robertson renders it be sober, and glosses it, be sober in thy head. Ellicott says the same and paraphrases it well: keep thy coolness and presence of mind, that thou be not entrapped into forgetfulness, but as one ever wakeful and ready, be on the watch. He takes the word to sum up the directions given since the middle of the previous chapter — to abstain from vain arguments, to avoid discussions likely to lead to strife, to be patient and gentle with all, to separate himself from merely nominal Christians, and to keep to the old paths in which the Apostles had walked. Gill keeps the watchman image and multiplies it: the charge relates to Timothy himself, his doctrine and conversation, and to others, to feed the flock under his care and know their state, to give the time of night and notice of approaching danger — whether in allusion to shepherds who watch their flocks night and day, or to watchmen upon the walls of cities, or to the priests and Levites in the temple. Wesley makes it an exercise of the whole soul: steadfast faith, patient hope, labouring love, unceasing prayer.

On the enduring of afflictions Clarke is brief and practical — let no sufferings affright thee, nor let the dread of them either cause thee to abandon the truth or relax in thy zeal for the salvation of men; and of the watching he adds that it is possible to be overtaken in a fault, to neglect one's duty and to lose one's soul, and that watching unto prayer prevents all these. Ellicott reminds Timothy of two things that should steady him in the suffering: what had been said earlier in the letter about the reward purposed for brave endurance, and the hard and faithful life of his master. Barnes takes the phrase about the evangelist to mean simply doing the work of preaching the gospel, or of one appointed to proclaim the glad tidings of salvation, which he calls the proper business of all ministers whatever other rank they may maintain. Clarke will have the term defined by the angel who first did that work, saying, behold, I evangelize unto you great joy which shall be to all people; and he presses the consequence that those who do not proclaim Christ as having tasted death for every man do not perform an evangelist's work, though as far as they preach the truth in sincerity God blesses them and their labours.

Ellicott adds a note on why the title is used here at all. The functions of a preacher and public teacher seem always to have been allotted to Timothy, a peculiar persuasive power of oratory being one of his chief gifts, and amid the many absorbing duties of his charge at Ephesus he must not neglect it. It is called the work of an evangelist to remind him that to perform it rightly needs zeal, close work, much study, thought and prayer; and it was by worthily performing those duties that the many turning aside would be best won back, hearing the great facts of the Gospel set beside the fables of the false teachers. The last charge Robertson renders fulfil, from a verb meaning to fill full, noting that Paul uses a plainer verb of the same sense when he speaks to Archippus about his ministry. Barnes reads it as furnishing full evidence of what the Christian ministry is designed to accomplish: Timothy was so to discharge the duties of his office as to give a fair illustration of what the ministry could do, and so to show the wisdom of the Saviour in instituting it. Clarke puts it as a challenge: push all thy principles to their utmost activity, and try what God will do for thee and by thee.
6:
The first verb has moved from possibility to fact. Robertson notes that Paul had used it in the Philippian letter of what might happen, whereas here what was then a possibility is now a certainty: the sacrifice of his life-blood has begun. Ellicott makes the same comparison — in his first imprisonment Paul looked on to a martyr's death as probable, and in his second he writes of the martyrdom as already beginning — and would render it more accurately, I am already being offered. Barnes objects that our version's word ready smuggles in an idea not in the Greek: the statement is merely that his death was about to occur, not that he was willing. The image is drawn from the wine and oil poured on the head of a victim about to be sacrificed, so that Paul is as one over whom the libation has already been poured, awaiting only the blow. Gill guards the figure carefully: this sacrifice of himself was not to atone for sin, Christ's death being the only and complete sacrifice for that, but was in the cause of Christ and for the confirmation of the Gospel.

The second figure is nautical. Barnes explains that the noun rendered departure comes from a verb meaning to loosen again, applied to casting off the fastenings of a ship before sailing, so that the idea is of one bound to this world as a ship to its moorings, whom death releases to spread his sails on the ocean of eternity; and he asks, with such a view of death, why should a Christian fear to die? Ellicott gives the same sense, the raising of the anchor and the loosing of the cables that held the vessel back from her voyage. Robertson observes that the word is our own analysis, and that the verb following is a perfect: the hour has struck. Ellicott adds why Paul chose so peaceful an image for a bloody death: he would not have Timothy, or the many who revered him, dismayed by his sufferings, but would show by his calm language that death was to him no terror but the appointed passage to glory — as the Master too spoke of his own approaching agony under a quiet, homely image. Wesley says only that God had undoubtedly shown him the time. Henry states two things plainly: the blood of the martyrs, though not a sacrifice of atonement, was a sacrifice of acknowledgment to the grace of God and his truth; and death to a good man is his release from the imprisonment of this world.

Three metaphors follow, and Ellicott separates them. The first is general, the combatant, the charioteer, the runner, with the description of the contest left undetermined; and the tense is remarkable, for the perfect says that the struggle had been bravely sustained in the past and was being equally bravely sustained to the end. The second narrows to the Olympic race-course; Chrysostom asks how Paul had finished his course and answers that he had made the circuit of the world, but Ellicott prefers the Apostle's own answer at Miletus, that his course was the ministry he had received of the Lord Jesus. The third changes the figure again, to a long, painful struggle to guard the treasure of the faith untarnished, now over, the sacred deposit handed on safe. Clarke reads all three from the Grecian games: he has wrestled that good wrestling and overcome in an honourable cause, has started for the prize and come up to the goal outstripping his competitors, and has kept the rules, for though a man overcome, yet is he not crowned except he strive lawfully. Robertson adds a curiosity from the stones: an inscription at Ephesus in which a man says, I have kept faith, and another saying of a man that he fought three fights and twice was crowned.
8:
Robertson takes the first word as an accusative meaning for the rest, and the verb as one used of a thing laid away in store, as elsewhere of the hope laid up in heaven. Barnes reads the same: the race has been run and the conflict waged, and all that remains of the whole career is that the crown be bestowed. Ellicott would render it the crown rather than a crown, and calls it the victory prize which the good fight of the preceding verse had won. Why it is called a crown of righteousness the three explain differently. Barnes takes it as won in the cause of righteousness and conferred as the reward of holiness — not the crown of ambition, nor a garland won in struggles for earthly distinction. Ellicott takes it as the crown to which righteousness can lay claim, that is, the crown awarded to righteousness. Gill takes it as the crown that comes through the righteousness of Christ, which gives the right to it, and which is possessed in a righteous way and not by force or usurpation as crowns sometimes are; he adds that the name may also express the perfect holiness of the heavenly state itself.

The judge is named with equal care. Clarke hears an allusion to the umpire at the Grecian games, whose office it was to declare the victor and give the crown. Robertson calls him the just judge, the umpire who makes no mistakes, who judges us all. Ellicott suggests a sharper contrast: not improbably the phrase was written against that unrighteous judge who had condemned Paul, and by whose unjust sentence he would presently suffer a painful death. Barnes draws the doctrine out of the title. It will be seen in the last day that the rewards of heaven are not conferred in an arbitrary manner, but because they ought to be — no man will be admitted to heaven who ought not, under all the circumstances of the case, to be admitted there, and no one will be excluded who ought to have been saved. Wesley reads the crown as of that righteousness which God has imputed to Paul and wrought in him. Clarke guards the whole against merit: here is a reward, but a reward not of debt but of grace, since it is by the grace of God that even an apostle is fitted for glory; and the crown is laid up, in view but not in possession, for we must die first.

The last clause opens the prize to everybody, and Barnes makes the most of it. This is not like the wreath of olive or laurel, conferred on one victor only; the struggle is not between Paul and a rival, so that if he obtains the crown another must be excluded. At those games only one could win, and all the rest, however skilfully they contended, were subjected to the mortification of failure; so it is with every prize this world bestows, in a lottery, in a class, in the scramble for office. Not so here: however numerous the competitors, all may obtain, all be crowned with a diadem of equal brilliancy, and none fails of the reward because another has it. Who then would not make an effort to win the immortal crown? Ellicott specifies the persons for whom it is reserved — those who in this life have longed for the appearance of the Lord in judgment, since none could truly desire it save his own, who love him and struggle to live his life; and he quotes Calvin, that Paul here excludes from the number of the faithful those to whom Christ's coming is a source of terror. Robertson notes that the participle is a perfect: who have loved and still love his appearing. Wesley says only a real Christian can love it.
9:
Chrysostom asks why Paul should summon Timothy at all, seeing he was entrusted with a church and a whole nation, and answers that it was not from arrogance: Paul had been ready enough to come to him, but was withholden by a strong necessity, no longer master of his own movements, in prison and all but on the point of death; and that this might not happen before he saw his disciple he sends for him, desiring to see him before he dies, and perhaps to deliver much in charge to him. Ellicott makes the same request an argument for the letter's genuineness. Who would ever have dreamed of putting such a summons into a forged letter, after those solemn verses in which the Apostle spoke of himself as already tasting the bitterness of death? But though a forger would never have thought of it, Paul might: he still lived, and the hope of life still burned; the martyrdom that seemed so close might be delayed, and days or months drag on and find him still languishing and solitary in his chains. Hoping against hope, he dictates the summons. Gill adds a second reason beside the loneliness: Paul had things to say about the care of the churches which he chose not to write with ink and paper.

Why haste was needed the others explain. Gill gives the winter coming on, when travelling would not be safe or comfortable, and the nearness of the apostle's death. Clarke thinks Paul wished Timothy to be present at his death, that he might have his faith confirmed by seeing how a Christian could die. Wesley makes the visit mutual, that Timothy might comfort him and be strengthened by him. Barnes draws a conclusion about Timothy's office from the summons: Paul plainly did not regard him as so confined to Ephesus that he might not go elsewhere if called by providence, and it is probable he obeyed, with no reason to believe he ever returned. Robertson notes that the vaguer word here is made definite later in the chapter, where Paul says before winter, so that the trial might apparently drag on through its various stages. Henry, who calls Timothy an evangelist rather than a fixed pastor of any one place, gives the plain reason from the next verse: Paul wanted Timothy's company and help, because several had left him. Luke indeed remained; and was not this enough? Paul did not think it so, for he loved the company of his friends.

Over the first of the departures they divide sharply. Henry takes it as apostasy from an ill principle: Demas quitted Paul and his interest, either for fear of suffering or being called off by secular affairs, his first love to Christ forsaken, and he fell in love with the world. Chrysostom reads it as ease rather than avarice — having loved his own security, he chose rather to live luxuriously at home than to suffer hardships and share the present danger — and notes that Paul blames him alone, not for the sake of blaming, but to confirm us, that we may not be effeminate in declining toils. Barnes will not have him made an example of worldliness at all: the phrase does not mean that he was avaricious or loved wealth or fame, but that he desired to live and would not stay and risk a martyr's death; there is perhaps a slight censure in Paul's language, the censure of grief, but no evidence of a love of gain or pleasure. Gill doubts that he apostatised, thinking his faith may have been right though low. Clarke complains that Demas has received little justice, since it is even fashionable to hunt him down, and floats the suggestion that all three men went as evangelists to their several fields. Ellicott dismisses as baseless the tradition that Demas became an idol priest at Thessalonica.
11:
Gill identifies the one companion who remained as the beloved physician who wrote the Gospel that bears his name and the Acts of the Apostles, a constant companion of Paul in his travels and sufferings. Barnes and Robertson say the same in fewer words, Robertson noting that Luke had been with Paul during the first Roman imprisonment also. Ellicott offers a reason for the closeness. Of all Paul's companions Luke seems to have been most closely associated with him, and most likely that long-continued intimacy was owing to the Apostle's weak and infirm health, to the dying body he ever bore about with him. He traces the association through the second and third missionary journeys, to Asia and to Jerusalem, through the captivity at Caesarea and the first imprisonment at Rome; and adds that Epiphanius speaks of Luke afterwards preaching chiefly in Gaul, and that a very general tradition includes him among the martyrs of the first age. Clarke supposes he continued with Paul even to his martyrdom. Wesley turns the word only into a consolation: of my fellow-labourers Luke alone is with me, but God is with me, and it is enough.

The request for Mark is read by all of them against the old quarrel. Barnes recalls the temporary alienation and says this passage proves it had been removed; and he suggests a motive. Paul felt that he was about to die, and if he suspected any lingering apprehension in Mark that the great apostle was not entirely reconciled, nothing would be more natural than to summon him to his side and express the kindest feeling towards him, since it would soothe any remaining irritation to receive such a message. Ellicott finds something strangely touching in it: the aged master bids Timothy bring on that last solemn journey the very man whom, a quarter of a century before, he had judged so severely, and on whose account he had separated from his old friend Barnabas. Since the hour when the young missionary's heart failed him in Pamphylia, Mark had by steady, earnest work won back his place. Robertson puts it plainly — Paul had long ago changed his opinion of Mark because Mark had changed his conduct and made good in his ministry, and now Paul longs to have the man he once scornfully rejected. Wesley says it in a line: who, though he once departed from the work, is now again profitable to me.

In what way Mark would be profitable is not said, and the guesses differ. Clarke takes it of service rather than of preaching — he would be very useful in ministering to the apostle in his close confinement — and doubts whether there was much public preaching at Rome just then. Ellicott reports Grotius's suggestion that the usefulness lay in Mark's knowledge of Latin, but thinks it likelier that he was serviceable as an assistant well acquainted with the details of Paul's many-sided work. Of the man sent away, Ellicott would render the connecting particle but rather than and, as referring to a suppressed thought: bring Mark, for I need one serviceable for the ministry; I had such a one in Tychicus, but he is gone. Neither the time nor the object of that journey is mentioned, though it probably fell some while before this letter. Barnes asks why Paul did not simply keep Tychicus with him, and answers that he had probably sent him before he saw reason to fear the worst, and that Tychicus had employment he could not leave. Clarke finds it strange to say I have sent him to Ephesus if Timothy was there, and supposes the sending was earlier. Gill reads it as care for the church: Tychicus was to supply Timothy's place, that Ephesus might not be without the ministry of the word in his absence.
13:
What the first article was, nobody is sure. Gill sets out the options: some take it for a dignified robe such as the consuls and senators of Rome wore, which he thinks unsuitable to the apostle; others for a coarser garment worn in cold and rainy weather, which, winter coming on, Paul now sends for, having left it at Troas in the summer; others for a kind of desk or chest to put papers and books in, as the Syriac renders it; and Jerome understood it of a book itself, the Hebrew volume of the Pentateuch. Barnes reports the same division and notes that the doubt is as old as Chrysostom, who says the word denotes a garment, though some understood by it a bag in which books were carried. Bloomfield, he adds, tries to unite the two by suggesting a cloak-bag in which the books and parchments had been left. Barnes himself judges the common opinion, a wrapper or travelling-cloak, the most probable, and remarks that such a garment would not be undesirable for a prisoner with winter approaching. Robertson agrees, noting that the papyri furnish many examples in that sense, and that Milligan, who had once argued for book-wrap, changed his mind.

Ellicott finds the request itself more puzzling than the word. Some have wished to make the garment a vestment worn in sacred functions; but such a supposition is in the highest degree precarious, since nowhere in the New Testament is the slightest hint given that any such vestment was used in the primitive Church. Far better to take it simply as a thick cloak or mantle left with Carpus at Troas, probably in summer, when Paul was disinclined to burden himself on a hurried journey with anything superfluous. Winter was now coming on, and the aged prisoner in the cold damp cell, with few friends and scant resources, remembered and wished for it. It is just such a request as a master would make of a disciple who knew his frail health, and one more mark of genuineness, since no forger would have dreamed of putting it down. Clarke reads the same wish differently — the books and parchments now sent for could not be for the apostle's own use, since he was on the eve of martyrdom, and he had probably intended to bequeath them to the faithful, that they might be preserved for the use of the Church. Wesley allows either the toga which belonged to Paul as a Roman citizen, or an upper garment needful as winter came on.

What the books and parchments were is guesswork, and each guesses. Barnes says it is worthy of remark that even Paul did not travel without books, and that he found them necessary for the work of the ministry; of the parchments he notes that the word means dressed skins, among the earliest materials for writing, and that these seem to have been something different from the books — Benson supposing letters Paul had received, Macknight the originals of those he had written, and Bishop Bull a kind of commonplace book into which he entered hints and extracts from his reading. Ellicott inclines to Bull's view for the parchments, taking them for notes gathered over many years of diligent study, which Paul would have with him as long as life remained; the books he supposes a few choice works, partly on Jewish sacred history and partly heathen writings, of which Paul was plainly a diligent student. He quotes Erasmus on the whole request — behold the Apostle's goods and movables, a poor cloak to keep him from the weather, and a few books. Robertson guesses copies of Old Testament books, possibly of Paul's own letters, perhaps even of the sayings of Christ; and he remarks that the old preacher can be happy with his books, and would not waste his time in prison.
14:
Who this man was they try to fix from the trade attached to his name. Barnes renders it brazier, though the word covers a worker in any metal, and identifies him probably with the Alexander delivered to Satan in the first letter. Gill takes him for the same, supposing he had lately been at Rome and was now returned to Ephesus, and that the trade is named to distinguish him from others and to show his insolence, since though an illiterate person in so mean a station he took upon him to resist the apostle and his doctrine. Clarke will not have him a tradesman at all, but a rabbin, since the Jews often applied the name of some trade as an epithet to their literary men. Ellicott, identifying him with the Alexander of the Ephesian tumult, makes him a Jew, one of those bitter, life-long antagonists of the Gentile Apostle who crossed his path at every step; and he passes on the suggestion that the enmity dated from days when Saul and Alexander both belonged to the strictest Pharisee party, the one afterwards becoming the Apostle of the Gentiles while the other remained a fanatic. Robertson doubts that identification unless the man afterwards became a Christian.

The words that follow have troubled readers, and the manuscripts offer an escape from them. Clarke reports that the best copies, several versions and some of the chief Greek fathers read not may the Lord reward him but he will reward, which makes the sentence declaratory rather than an imprecation, and thinks this most like the spirit of that heavenly man. Ellicott and Robertson adopt the future without argument, and Wesley says simply that Paul spoke it prophetically. Barnes keeps the received reading and defends it. This need not be an expression of private feeling, still less a desire for revenge; it is the language of one who wished God to treat the man exactly as he ought to be treated, which may accord with the highest benevolence. It is the aim of every just government that everyone should be treated as he deserves, and a police officer, a judge, a juryman might pray so with no malevolent feeling toward any human being. Barnes notes that the variant readings themselves arose from a belief that the common text expressed a sentiment inconsistent with the spirit of a Christian, and a wish to find a better.

What the injury was, all agree it was public rather than personal. Barnes reads the warning as showing that Alexander was still a public teacher whose discourses were plausible and artful, so that the best and wisest of men need to be on their guard against the advocates of error; and the phrase our words, which the margin renders preachings, makes it clear that the harm was done to the cause of truth and not to Paul privately. Ellicott thinks it probable that Alexander had been at Rome and had given evidence against Paul and argued against his defence, and reports that some understand the phrase of that defence before the imperial tribunal. Robertson renders the two clauses tightly — keep thyself away from him, for he stood against my words. Clarke supposes the man travelled about from place to place for the purpose of opposing the Gospel, being put forward by the Jews, and calls him a constant opposer of Christian doctrine. Gill advises shunning his company altogether, that he might have no opportunity of doing hurt either to Timothy or to the church at Ephesus. Henry draws the general lesson: there is as much danger from false brethren as from open enemies, and it is dangerous having to do with those who would be enemies to such a man as Paul.
16:
The word rendered answer is our own apology in its older sense. Clarke says it properly signifies a defence or vindication, and is the word from which the apologies of the primitive fathers took their name, those being vindications of Christianity. Robertson notes the same, and says there is really no way to decide whether the first defence means the opening stage of the present trial or the earlier trial that ended in acquittal, though he inclines to the first. Barnes weighs the same question and observes the difficulty: if Paul had already had a trial during this imprisonment, it is hard to see why he was still held a prisoner. Gill states plainly what happened at it — when Paul made his first defence against the charges laid against him in one of the courts of Rome, no man appeared in his cause to speak to his character, to be a witness for him, or to plead for him. Robertson renders the Greek closely: no one came by my side; and of the second verb, whose tense the manuscripts vary, he offers either they were forsaking me one by one, or they left me all at once.

Why they stayed away is explained from the times. Ellicott describes what was wanting: no friend stood by him, no advocate pleaded his cause, no procurator helped him arrange and sift the evidence, no patron of a noble house gave him countenance. The position of a well-known Christian leader accused in those years was critical, and the friend who dared stand by him would himself be in great danger; for after the great fire the Christians were looked on as enemies of the state and charged as the authors of that disaster, Nero allowing them to be condemned as incendiaries to avert suspicion from himself, and a great persecution following. Clarke describes that persecution: the victims wrapped in pitched clothes, chained to a stake and set alight to give light in the streets at night, as the satirist he quotes alludes. Barnes takes the desertion as an instance of a common thing: to forsake a friend in the day of calamity is not uncommon, and Paul experienced what thousands before and since have done — as Job was forsaken by kindred and household, and the Psalmist by his familiar friends, and the Saviour himself in his trials. Much professed friendship is false, he says, and calamity is a test it cannot abide.

The prayer that closes the verse strikes them most. Henry sets it beside the sentence passed on Alexander a few lines earlier and sees a distinction between sins of presumption and sins of infirmity: against the man who maliciously withstood him Paul says, the Lord reward him according to his works; but of these Christians, who through weakness shrank from him in the time of trial, he says, let it not be laid to their charge. It was their sin not to appear for him, but a sin of weakness and therefore the more excusable; God might justly lay it to their charge, and Paul by his prayer endeavours to prevent it. Clarke prefers the Greek to any English rendering: let it not be placed to their account, let them not reckon for it with the supreme Judge at the great day. Barnes says the prayer breathes the very spirit of Christ, and compares the words from the cross and those of Stephen. Ellicott adds the reason for the gentleness: Paul knew that to stand by him then was a service of the greatest danger, and these were weak, unnerved friends who deserted him through no ill-will to the cause but solely from timidity — as his own Master, in his hour of peril, had been left alone. Wesley asks the question the verse raises: do we expect to find such as will not forsake us?
17:
Gill sets the presence against the absence just described: it was what Christ himself had not when he was forsaken by his disciples, and the presence of God is more than all friends whatever, often enjoyed by the believer just when they drop him. Clarke says that when all human help failed God interposed the more remarkably, so that the excellency plainly appeared to be of God and not of man. Barnes takes it for a universal truth about the faithfulness of God. Robertson renders the verb closely — the Lord took his stand by my side — and thinks Jesus appeared to Paul at this crisis as he had done so many times before; of the second verb he says it means that power was poured into him. Ellicott adds what the strengthening was for: the felt presence of his Lord gave him courage and readiness, so that alone, friendless, accused of a hateful crime before the highest earthly tribunal in the capital of the world, he was enabled to plead not only for himself but for the cause with which he was identified.

What the trial accomplished divides them a little. Ellicott and Robertson render the clause not that the preaching might be fully known but that it might be fully performed or proclaimed; Ellicott judges the occasion the culminating point of Paul's labours, the last stone of the laborious edifice of his life's work, and thinks that had his courage failed then, the spirit of the sorely-tried Church of Rome must have sunk. Barnes keeps the received sense, that the gospel might obtain full credence: forsaken by all men, Paul was so steadfast and so calm in the prospect of death that all who witnessed the trial saw religion was a reality. He turns it into a general observation: one of the chief means of establishing the gospel has been the testimony of martyrs, and men judge justly of a religion by its power to sustain the soul when entering an untried state of being. Of the hearers, Barnes notes that Rome was then the centre of the world, so that the knowledge of Paul's sufferings might be carried by strangers to the ends of the earth; Ellicott hears in the phrase a further reference to those uncounted peoples in the isles of the Gentiles who would come by Paul's words to the knowledge of the truth. Clarke observes that the same preaching must have endeared him to some while incensing others.

Who or what the lion was, none of them will settle. Clarke calls the phrase a proverbial form of speech for the most imminent danger; Barnes allows either Nero under the figure or literally the beasts of the amphitheatre; Robertson leaves it open between Nero, Satan and the arena, remarking that a Roman citizen could not lawfully be sent to the lions; and Ellicott takes it simply as a figure for extreme peril, citing Ignatius, who described his own journey to Rome as one long fight with wild beasts and called his soldier guards ten leopards. What follows is not a hope of escaping death. Barnes is careful: Paul does not say from death, for he expected now to die, but he was assured God would keep him from shrinking from it when the hour came, and from apostasy. Ellicott rejects even that as foreign to the spirit of a letter in which there is not one note of fear, and which reads in places like a triumphant song of death; he would supply after every evil work the words of the enemies, and understand that through this very death the Lord would bring him safe into the heavenly kingdom. Wesley puts both halves in a phrase — far more than delivering me from death, and a kingdom far better than that of Nero.
19:
Ellicott gives the fullest account of the first pair greeted. Originally of Pontus, they had settled at Rome, where Aquila exercised his trade of tent-maker; driven out by the decree of Claudius which banished the Jews, they came to Corinth, where Paul became acquainted with them, though they were evidently Christians already when he first met them. He traces them at Corinth, at Ephesus, and back at Rome, and counts them among the active teachers of the first days of the faith — their ability shown by the fact that from them the eloquent Alexandrian, Apollos, learnt to be a Christian. That the wife is named first, here and elsewhere, Ellicott takes to hint that she was the principal worker of the two, and he sets her among that band of devoted women whom the preaching of Christ had called into existence. Gill notes only that they were of the same occupation with the apostle, and that he had left them at Ephesus and they seem still to have been there. Of the household next greeted, Clarke and Ellicott both conclude from the form of the greeting that Onesiphorus himself was by then dead, his family remaining at Ephesus.

Two absences are then explained. Gill and Clarke agree that the first man was chamberlain, or treasurer, of Corinth, and had been sent with Timothy into Macedonia, whence he probably returned to his own city and settled there. Barnes observes that there seems to have been some expectation that he would accompany Paul to Rome, but that reasons had occurred for his remaining, and that his doing so is mentioned without blame. Ellicott distinguishes two men of the name among Paul's friends, one a resident official at Corinth and the other one of the travelling band. Of the second absence Ellicott suggests the mention was meant to clear the man of any charge of neglect: the one remained at Corinth, but the other's reason for not coming to Rome was his sickness. Clarke and Wesley both take the sickness for evidence about miracles — even the apostles could not work them when they pleased, that power being given rarely and for special purposes, and only when God pleased. Clarke adds a reconstruction of the journey that ended in prison: from Macedonia to Corinth, thence to Troas, where Paul lodged with Carpus, thence to Ephesus, thence to Miletus, and from Miletus by sea to Rome.

The renewed summons is dated. Gill takes the urgency kindly, as consulting Timothy's good as well as Paul's advantage, since travelling later would not be safe. Clarke gives two reasons, that the apostle's time was short and uncertain, and that sailing in those seas was dangerous in winter, adding that whether Timothy reached him before the martyrdom is not known. Robertson finds the detail pathetic if Paul was then in the Mamertine dungeon with winter coming on and without the cloak he had asked for. Of the four names that follow, Barnes says only that they are common in the classic writers and that of the persons meant we know nothing; Clarke reports the traditions that make two of them bishops of Rome and finds no sufficient ground for the claims. Ellicott is readier to identify them: he takes the third for the first of the long line of bishops of Rome, whose consecration falls in the year of the martyrdom, and thinks it fair to suppose it one of the Apostle's dying acts; and some, he reports, identify the other two with a Pudens and a Claudia named by Martial, the one a senator's son and the other called a Briton. Of the closing benediction Clarke observes that it is a prayer addressed to Christ by one of the most eminent of his apostles, and so a proof against the assertion that prayer is never offered to Christ in the New Testament.
